defaults.permitted_development: A garden room can usually be permitted development in Scotland where it remains incidental to the house, sits within the curtilage and complies with the Class 3A limits for ancillary buildings. It should not operate as a separate dwelling.

rules.height_rules: A common Scottish benchmark is eaves up to 3m, up to 4m overall and no more than 2.5m overall for any part within 1m of the boundary.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate garden-room depth allowance in Scotland. What matters is curtilage position, not building forward of an elevation fronting a road and leaving at least half of the relevant curtilage undeveloped.
rules.boundary_rules: The room cannot be forward of a principal elevation or a side elevation fronting a road, and anything within 1m of the boundary should stay at or below 2.5m overall.
rules.roof_rules: Permitted development works best for a simple single-storey garden room. Terrace-style roofs, upper-storey accommodation and overtly house-like forms move the proposal away from the ordinary ancillary-building route.
rules.materials_rules: The room should remain ancillary and not be laid out or used as self-contained accommodation. Visible materials should stay restrained, especially where conservation area or listed-building limits apply.

rules.permitted_development: Scottish householder rights can often cover a modest garden room where it stays ancillary to the dwellinghouse, follows the Class 3A siting and height limits and does not become self-contained living accommodation.

rules.height_rules: Keep the room within the Scottish Class 3A height envelope: eaves no more than 3m, an overall maximum of 4m and a 2.5m overall cap where any part sits within 1m of the boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Garden rooms are not controlled by a standalone projection figure in Scotland. The main tests are where the building sits in the curtilage and whether more than half of the relevant curtilage would remain undeveloped.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and road-facing siting are the main Scottish checks. Keep the room out of forward road-facing positions and design around the 2.5m overall cap where any part sits within 1m of the boundary.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof low-key and subordinate. The Scottish ancillary-building route is aimed at a modest single-storey room rather than a terrace-style or upper-floor design.
rules.materials_rules: Materials can be modern, but the room should still read as a subordinate domestic outbuilding rather than a separate residence. Sensitive Scottish settings usually call for the most restrained visible finish.

restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent is required in Scotland for demolition, extension or material alteration of a listed building, inside or out, where character is affected.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.permitted_development: In Scotland, a garden room can often use the ordinary ancillary-building route if it remains incidental to the house, stays within the relevant garden-ground limits and does not function as a separate residence.

rules.height_rules: The usual Scottish garden-room limits are eaves up to 3m, an overall height up to 4m and no more than 2.5m overall if any part of the structure is within 1m of the boundary.
rules.depth_rules: Instead of a fixed depth limit, Scottish Class 3A looks at siting within the curtilage, avoiding forward road-facing positions and retaining at least half of the relevant curtilage undeveloped.
rules.boundary_rules: The most important Scottish siting points are road-facing position and boundary proximity. A room close to the boundary should stay within the 2.5m overall cap and should not project into a forward road-facing position.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form matters because it can make the structure read like a second dwelling. A simple, subordinate single-storey roof is much safer than a dominant or house-like design.
rules.materials_rules: A Scottish garden room can use contemporary or traditional finishes, but it should still look subordinate to the dwellinghouse and remain incidental in use rather than self-contained.
